Photograph: Lisi Niesner/Reuters Climate crisis UK to join EU ocean science scheme to better predict extreme weather events Cooperation on OceanEye, which aims to create ‘real-time’ model of world’s oceans, comes amid efforts to boost EU ties UK politics live – latest updates Europe live – latest updates Karen McVeigh Wed 23 Sep 2026 10.24 EDT Last modified on Wed 23 Sep 2026 10.45 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Britain is to join a major new ocean science programme, led by the EU, to better forecast extreme weather and climate events, the environment secretary is to announce in New York. The announcement on Wednesday will come as Andy Burnham’s government aims to rebuild the UK’s relationship with Europe, and follows warnings this year’s “supersized” El Niño, tracked in the Pacific Ocean , will fuel more extreme weather globally. Scientists have warned that the global marine monitoring system, which is vital to predict extreme weather events and ultimately to save lives, is under strain after threats by the US administration this year to dismantle its substantial share of global ocean observations. In June, the EU launched a €92m (£78m) initiative called OceanEye , to boost its role in ocean observation and to provide data-backed marine intelligence to deepen understanding and management of the ocean. It plans to create a digital “real time” replica model of the ocean, collected by satellites, sensors and other models by 2030, to help decisions on ocean protection and security. The EU introduced an international alliance with Canada as part of OceanEye, to address critical gaps in under-monitored regions and strengthen cooperation between nations. In addition to weather and climate predictions, ocean observations also underpin national security, global trade and marine protections. Angela Eagle will announce the UK is to join the scheme at a meeting attended by the European Commission president, Ursula von der Leyen, and Mark Carney, Canada’s prime minister, at the UN headquarters in New York. Britain will share more data from the Met Office and other agencies with the EU and Canada than before. The environment secretary will tell the event: “As an island nation and a global leader in climate science, we know that data from ocean monitoring is essential to our ability to protect and restore our oceans, and anticipate and respond to the huge threats they face, because we cannot save our oceans if we do not understand them.” “Changing weather patterns and currents are fuelling the extreme weather which is already impacting all of our nations – through floods, droughts, storms and extreme heat. That’s why the UK is so committed to maintaining our vital global network of observation systems, which span coastal waters, shelf seas and the open ocean, including some of the longest-running observations in the world.” skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to First Edition Our morning email breaks down the key stories of the day, telling you what’s happening and why it matters after newsletter promotion Joining the alliance to support and provide data to the Global Ocean Observing System (GOOS) would help better protect Britain from the impacts of climate change, said the Department for Environment, Food and Rural Affairs. Currently, the global ocean observing capacity has significant gaps, at the poles, the deep ocean and of biological measurements. The US, which provides over half the ocean observing platforms and much of the technology, has reversed a proposal to scrap its $368m (£275m) funding for its Ocean Observatories Initiative after a backlash from scientists. However, moves to cut funding for US ocean agencies have left GOOS vulnerable to changing priorities of the US administration. Beállítom Bódis Tamás pályacsúccsal, 19 óra 40 perc 51 másodperces idővel nyerte meg a Spartathlont, az Athén és Spárta közötti 246 kilométeres ultramaratont. Bódis idén több kiugró eredménnyel a háta mögött vágott neki a klasszikus görög ultrának, pályacsúccsal győzött az Ultrabalatonon , egy lengyelországi versenyen 11 percet faragott a 100 kilométer országos csúcsán, majd júliusban a pokoli hőség miatt is rettenetesen nehéz kaliforniai Badwateren harmadik helyet ért el. A magyar ultrafutó legnagyobb ellenfelének a görög Ziszimpulosz Fotisz ígérkezett, aki 2021 és 2024 között négyszer győzött, és egészen eddig övé volt a pályacsúcs. A 2019-ben egyszer már nyerő Bódist most nem tudta veszélyeztetni, a magyar futó 15 percet javított a pályacsúcson. A görög 52 perces hátrányban érkezett meg a második helyen. Az 1983 óta megrendezett Spartathlont a férfiaknál eddig két magyar tudta megnyerni korábban, az már említett Bódis, illetve 1991-ben Bogár János. A nőknél több magyar siker született, Lubics Szilvia háromszor (2011, 2013, 2014), Nagy Katalin (2015, 2016) és Maráz Zsuzsanna (2018, 2019) kétszer, Mórocza Andrea (2025) egyszer tudott nyerni . A Spartathlon története az ókorig nyúlik vissza. A legenda szerint időszámításunk előtt 490-ben egy Pheidippidész nevű futár másfél nap alatt jutott el futva, gyalogolva Athénból Spártába, hogy ott segítséget kérjen a perzsák elleni háborúhoz. Hogy valóban lehetséges gyalogszerrel 36 óra alatt megtenni a 246 kilométeres távolságot a két nagyváros között, azt 1982-ben saját emberkísérletével igazolta John Foden, a brit légierő tisztje. Egy évvel később pedig már meg is rendezték az első, a mai napig amatőr alapokon nyugvó versenyt, amelynek most a 42. kiadása volt. https://www.perthnow.com.au/lifestyle/mo.text: The Skoda Peaq lives up to its name. According to company bosses, this large, luxurious, seven-seat electric SUV will take the Czech brand to a whole new level – the new EV representing the peak of its expertise, if you will. Wearing the latest iteration of Skoda’s ‘Modern Solid’ design philosophy, which has already been seen on the much smaller and similarly new Epiq electric SUV, the Peaq is a smart-looking family mover thanks in part to the firm’s first flush-fitting door handles. Whether you think they’re a good or a bad thing, they contribute to one seriously aerodynamic form – despite the Peaq’s bulk, it has a coefficient of drag as low as 0.249Cd at its slipperiest. Available with two battery sizes, a choice of outputs and the ability to have two driven wheels or four, the three-row Peaq competes with any decent seven-seat EV you can think of, including ostensibly premium (and much dearer rivals) such as the Volvo EX90. But, really, the main two targets in the Skoda’s crosshairs will be the excellent Korean duo, in the forms of the Hyundai Ioniq 9 and the Kia EV9. We went to the Alpine borders of Germany and Austria to sample the Skoda Peaq for the first time and see if it has what it takes. How much does the Skoda Peaq cost? Prices and trim specifications for the Skoda Peaq in Australia have not yet been set ahead of its likely arrival here in 2027, but the SUV is going to be expensive. The dearest model ranges Skoda currently sells here are the Superb Wagon (up to $69,690 before on-road costs), the Kodiaq large SUV (up to $70,590 plus ORCs) and the Enyaq Coupe (up to $77,590 plus ORCs), and it’s evident the Peaq is going to be positioned beyond those. If it could come in at less than $100,000, that would give it an edge over both the EV9 and the Ioniq 9, both of which have starting prices into six figures. But even if Skoda's new flagship SUV starts in the $90,000s (or less), top-grade variants with all the trimmings are almost certainly going to be priced beyond $100k. The question is, by how much? What is the Skoda Peaq like on the inside? At 4874mm long, and with nearly three metres of that (2965mm) packed in between its axles, the Skoda Peaq is a big beast and that contributes to a healthy air of interior spaciousness – with the company claiming the passenger compartment was created to mimic the comfort levels of a lounge. We’ll come back to that point shortly, but in terms of material finishing and tech integration, the Peaq’s fascia is a winner. Everything looks and feels superb, and what switches there are operate with a deeply satisfying tactility, while the 13.6-inch Android-powered infotainment touchscreen is a fine system. The Peaq does run much of its in-car climate systems through the screen, unfortunately, but it always keeps the key features in a strip at the bottom of the display. And there are three rocker tabs down above the twin MagSafe wireless phone charging pads that control the two front zones of temperature, plus fan speed. Neatly, when you make your side of the cabin hotter, an LED line in the switch briefly glows red, and if you go cooler it shines blue. In other regards, there’s acres of space in row two of the Peaq, and even the sort of seating that should see three people able to sit side-by-side there, but the chairs in the final row are better suited to children and smaller people. The pay-off for that is the big Skoda EV has a minimum of 299 litres of boot space, even with a full complement of human passengers. That number increases to a vast 890L with the sixth and seventh seats folded away, and a simply gigantic 2075L in two-seat format. If that’s not enough, there’s 37L of under-bonnet storage as well. Sitting above the passenger seats is, for Peaq variants with it equipped, the largest panoramic sunroof Skoda has yet fitted to one of its production cars. Practicality-wise, there are lots of storage solutions and spaces throughout the cabin, as well as plenty of Skoda’s proprietary ‘Simply Clever’ touches – including a dedicated option pack of these helpful items if you want it. The Peaq is also fitted as standard with a next-generation heat pump to maximise its electrical efficiency, while it also comes with bidirectional charging with vehicle-to-load (V2L) and vehicle-to-home (V2H) capabilities, although the latter requires a compatible bi-directional DC wallbox to work. But the star showing is the Relax Package. Skoda says this transforms the Peaq into a “lounge on wheels” and it includes power-adjustable, heated front seats with a massage function and ergonomic certification from German back-health organisation AGR. It also bundles in a 16-speaker, 755-Watt Sonos sound system, extendable legrests for the front seats which come out a long, long way, and even Velcro-on cushions for the head restraints. We could question the safety logic of reclining the driver to such an extent that they’re almost lying down behind the wheel, then giving them a massage, a warming device and a pillow, but there is no arguing with how comfortable these seats are in practice – this might be the most cosseting and relaxing driver’s chair in any vehicle we’ve ever sat in. And as if that wasn’t enough, the Relax Package also comes with a neat trick, allowing you to make a table out of the front cupholders in just a few easy actions. What's under the bonnet? Three initial variants of the Skoda Peaq are available: two single-motor, rear-driven machines, and a range-topping dual-motor, all-wheel drive version. Things kick off with the Peaq 60, which has a 150kW/350Nm rear-mounted APP350 motor. Weighing in at 2156-2279kg, Skoda reckons this entry-level model of its biggest SUV will do the 0-100km/h sprint in 8.5 seconds and top out at 160km/h. The Peaq 90 retains a single motor on the rear axle, but it’s the newer, more potent APP550 propulsion unit that has been seen in several other Volkswagen Group EVs in recent years. This generates up to 210kW and 545Nm, enough to punch the 2334-2449kg Peaq 90 from 0-100km/h in a claimed 7.1 seconds, while the top speed increases to 180km/h. Finally, the Peaq 90x we’re trying here is all-wheel drive, but surprisingly it reverts to the APP350 motor at the back. So even though Skoda won’t officially quote a combined torque output for this dual-motor drivetrain, if you add its two motors’ torque together, it still has less of the stuff (484Nm) than the rear-drive 90. However, power climbs to 220kW and with the added traction advantages of all-wheel drive, the 90x is the fastest-accelerating Peaq of the lot with a claimed 6.8-second time. Its top speed remains the same as that of the 90 – and it weighs in at a startling 2407-2529kg. Incidentally, all Peaqs can tow, with the rear-drive models rated at 1800kg of braked trailer, while the AWD 90x increases that to 2000kg. Both batteries used in the Peaq family are nickel-manganese-cobalt (NMC) items, with the 60 model the only one so far to use the smaller pack, rated at 63kWh gross and 59kWh usable for a quoted range of 459km. Its peak DC-charging speed is 160kW, which means a 10-80 per cent top-up requires 27 minutes. The pair of 90 cars, though, whether fitted with one motor or two, run the larger 91kWh gross, 86kWh net unit, with a maximum 199kW DC rate. The significantly larger capacity of this battery pack means the 10-80 per cent charge is marginally longer at 28 minutes, but the official distance these variants can go between charges stands at 647km for the single-motor version and 613km for this AWD 90x. All Skoda Peaqs have a fastest AC charging rate of 11kW, resulting in a 6.5-hour 10-100 per cent charging time for the 60, and nine hours exactly for both the 90 and 90x. Those times would extend to around nine and something beyond 12.5 hours, respectively, on a more typical 7.4kW domestic wallbox. How does the Skoda Peaq drive? Let’s get the major negative out of the way first: the Skoda Peaq 90x is not a machine which likes to be hustled. Even in Sportline trim, with Dynamic Chassis Control (DCC) variable dampers fitted, the Peaq feels ill at ease if you start hammering it into corners in an enthusiastic fashion. There’s too much body movement and a general air of the whole car straining to contain its not-inconsiderable mass that takes the shine off the handling. But nowhere does the Skoda betray its sheer mass more obviously than when you are on the brakes. Unlike its pint-size Epiq cousin at the other end of the manufacturer’s EV lineup, the Peaq makes do with drums on the rear axle, rather than discs, and this leads to a brake pedal that can be quite mushy underfoot. Indeed, approaching one left-turn junction on our test drive at a reasonable 80km/h, when we started trying to slow down for the turn a good distance out, we realised we had to bleed more and more and more pedal pressure on, because the Peaq was simply not slowing down. A firmer and slightly panicked prod of the left-side pedal was finally required to prevent us missing the turn and sailing on down the road. So, the Skoda is not great for handling, although because it is grippy, reasonably composed overall and blessed with positive, communicative steering, it’s also by no means actively bad in this department either. Happily, there’s an enormous pay-off. We can’t think of many vehicles this side of $150,000 which ride better than a Skoda Peaq fitted with DCC adaptive damping. It is astounding how graceful, how utterly subdued, and how relaxing this SUV is on the move. It doesn’t matter whether you're in town, out on the open road, or cruising along a freeway at 110km/h and more, the king Skoda is imperiously sumptuous and enormously refined. It’s an absolute delight. And it manages such dignified grace in all conditions, even when it’s running on a set of whopping 21-inch alloy wheels. We want to get a Peaq on our home roads as soon as we can to see if it can replicate this glassy, unruffled showing on our patch as well, but based on our initial drive all we can say about this grand Skoda EV is that this is precisely how you want a family-conveying machine like this to ride. It’s magnificent. What do you get? We’re still awaiting confirmation of the specifications for Australian-market Skoda Peaqs, but we’d expect even the base-grade variant to come with the following equipment as standard. 2027 Skoda Peaq equipment highlights: Is the Skoda Peaq safe? The Skoda Peaq hasn’t yet been assessed by either ANCAP or Euro NCAP, although it comes with a standard roster of advanced driver-assistance systems (ADAS) including traffic jam assist, front assist with emergency braking (vehicles, pedestrians and cyclists), lane assist and emergency assist, blind-spot detection with door exit warning, turn assist, crossroad assist, traffic sign recognition, crew protect assist, and speed assist, among more. How much does the Skoda Peaq cost to run? Skoda Australia provides an excellent seven-year, unlimited-distance warranty with two years of roadside assistance – a level of cover which is automatically extended for another 24 months every time you have the car serviced at an official Skoda dealer. Skoda also recommends its EVs are serviced on a longer, biennial schedule than its combustion-powered cars, making a Peaq look much more tempting than a Kodiaq. During our test, the only slight question mark was around real-world efficiency, as the Peaq 90x Sportline returned 21.8kWh/100km across a 190km mixed-roads route in warm, dry conditions. That’s some way off its official figure of 15.8kWh/100km, but in mitigation it did spend a good portion of that test route heading towards its 180km/h limiter on the autobahn, as well as climbing some Austrian Alps later in the day for good measure. Even at that rate of consumption, an easy 400km between charges ought to be possible, yet we think only moderately gentler and more sympathetic driving in representative conditions will see the Peaq hitting 500km or more at a time, all year round. CarExpert's Take on the Skoda Peaq While we await pricing for the Skoda Peaq, we’re nevertheless more than impressed enough by this newest, grandest Czech EV to proclaim it among the class-leaders in its market segment. Okay, so it doesn’t like a taxing workout on a challenging road, it can feel hefty on its at-times spongy brakes, and for all its exterior size you’re still not going to get adults of an above-average height to sit comfortably in row three of its cabin. But if you want a car that is nigh-on unbeatable for rolling refinement and unflappable ride comfort, the Skoda Peaq is the only car for you. As family transportation goes, it absolutely smashes its design brief into smithereens, because it’s a genuinely brilliant seven-seat electric wagon. CarExpert can save you thousands on a new Skoda.
